name: Flax-Flower Blue
lede: Flax-flower blue is a soft, slightly purplish blue, number 30 among the blues of Werner's nomenclature of colors, where it is tied to a butterfly, the flax flower and a blue copper ore.

sections.title: A number in Werner's blues
sections.body: The name belongs to the color standard of the German mineralogist Abraham Werner, which Patrick Syme turned into a standard for naturalists in his own editions [1]. Our library files it as Werner no. 30 among the blues [2]. Baty's *Nature's Palette* pairs most standards with an animal, a vegetable and a mineral example, and for this one it gives the light parts of the wing margin of a butterfly called the Devil's butterfly, the flax flower, and blue copper ore [1]. Its neighbors show the method: no. 29, ultramarine blue, is the small blue Heath butterfly, borage, and lapis lazuli, and no. 31, Berlin blue, is the jay's wing feather, hepatica and blue sapphire [1].

sections.title: The plates
sections.body: Baty illustrates names with period plates [1]. Flax-flower blue is shown at the edges of the wings of a small tortoiseshell in Knorr's *Deliciae naturae selectae* (1766), on the petals of a perennial flax in an 1863 watercolor of *Linum perenne*, and on azurite in Schubert's natural history (1886) [1]. Baty cautions that the swatches and plates have grown more muted with time [1]. The swatch on this page is therefore an aged, approximate scan of Werner no. 30, and not a measurement of a living flax petal [2][1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: This swatch is a light purplish blue, 6 units from ISCC-NBS block 195, and Maerz and Paul (1930) record the name from 1814 [2]. Its nearest named neighbors include [[cornflower]], [[dusty-blue]] and [[denim]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Colors close to it appear in 193 of our 23,781 paintings, 0.8 per cent, more than for 61 per cent of the named colors [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 38 per cent of the 111 paintings where the palette lens finds it [3]. It is most common in the 1900s, in 17 of 1,674 paintings from then, 1.4 times the museums' baseline [3].

The painter most devoted to it is Claude Monet, who has it in 4 of 50 works here, 6.5 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [3]. The earliest match in the archive is by Rogier van der Weyden, about 1440, and the early centuries are thin, so that is a floor [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test [3].
